The weight matrices are taken from\\\\nthe 48th layer of GPT-3.\\\\nWe draw several conclusions from Table 7. First, ∆W has a stronger correlation with W compared\\\\nto a random matrix, indicating that ∆W ampliﬁes some features that are already in W. Second,\\\\ninstead of repeating the top singular directions of W, ∆W only ampliﬁes directions that are not\\\\nemphasized in W. Third, the ampliﬁcation factor is rather huge: 21.5 ≈6.91/0.32 for r = 4.\\\\nSee Section H.4 for why r = 64 has a smaller ampliﬁcation factor. We also provide a visualization\\\\nin Section H.3 for how the correlation changes as we include more top singular directions from Wq.\\\\nThis suggests that the low-rank adaptation matrix potentially ampliﬁes the important features for\\\\nspeciﬁc downstream tasks that were learned but not emphasized in the general pre-training model.\\\\n8\\\\nCONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK\\\\nFine-tuning enormous language models is prohibitively expensive in terms of the hardware required\\\\nand the storage/switching cost for hosting independent instances for different tasks. We propose\\\\nLoRA, an efﬁcient adaptation strategy that neither introduces inference latency nor reduces input\\\\nsequence length while retaining high model quality. Importantly, it allows for quick task-switching\\\\nwhen deployed as a service by sharing the vast majority of the model parameters. While we focused\\\\non Transformer language models, the proposed principles are generally applicable to any neural\\\\nnetworks with dense layers.\\\\nThere are many directions for future works. 1) LoRA can be combined with other efﬁcient adapta-\\\\ntion methods, potentially providing orthogonal improvement. 2) The mechanism behind ﬁne-tuning\\\\nor LoRA is far from clear – how are features learned during pre-training transformed to do well\\\\non downstream tasks? We believe that LoRA makes it more tractable to answer this than full ﬁne-\\\\n12\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 13 ---\\\\ntuning. 3) We mostly depend on heuristics to select the weight matrices to apply LoRA to. Are\\\\nthere more principled ways to do it? 4) Finally, the rank-deﬁciency of ∆W suggests that W could\\\\nbe rank-deﬁcient as well, which can also be a source of inspiration for future works.\\\\nREFERENCES\\\\nArmen Aghajanyan, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Sonal Gupta. Consequently,\\\\nadapter layers must be computed in addition to the base model, inevitably introducing additional\\\\nlatency. While as pointed out in R¨uckl´e et al. (2020), the latency introduced by adapter layers can\\\\nbe mitigated when the model batch size and/or sequence length is large enough to full utilize the\\\\nhardware parallelism. We conﬁrm their observation with a similar latency study on GPT-2 medium\\\\nand point out that there are scenarios, notably online inference where the batch size is small, where\\\\nthe added latency can be signiﬁcant.\\\\nWe measure the latency of a single forward pass on an NVIDIA Quadro RTX8000 by averaging\\\\nover 100 trials. We vary the input batch size, sequence length, and the adapter bottleneck dimension\\\\nr. We test two adapter designs: the original one by Houlsby et al. (2019), which we call AdapterH,\\\\nand a recent, more efﬁcient variant by Lin et al. (2020), which we call AdapterL. See Section 5.1\\\\nfor more details on the designs. We plot the slow-down in percentage compared to the no-adapter\\\\nbaseline in Figure 5.\\\\n0\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\n20\\\\n25\\\\n30\\\\n35\\\\n0\\\\n10\\\\n100\\\\n250\\\\nAdapterH r\\\\nSeq Len = 128\\\\nSeq Len = 256\\\\nSeq Len = 512\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n0\\\\n10\\\\n100\\\\n250\\\\nAdapterL r\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\nFigure 5: Percentage slow-down of inference latency compared to the no-adapter (r = 0) baseline.\\\\nThe top row shows the result for AdapterH and the bottom row AdapterL. We tweak the colormap for better visibility.\\\\nC\\\\nDATASET DETAILS\\\\nGLUE Benchmark is a wide-ranging collection of natural language understanding tasks. It includes\\\\nMNLI (inference, Williams et al. (2018)), SST-2 (sentiment analysis, Socher et al. (2013)), MRPC\\\\n(paraphrase detection, Dolan & Brockett (2005)), CoLA (linguistic acceptability, Warstadt et al.\\\\n(2018)), QNLI (inference, Rajpurkar et al. (2018)), QQP8 (question-answering), RTE (inference),\\\\n8https://quoradata.quora.com/First-Quora-Dataset-Release-Question-Pairs\\\\n17\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 18 ---\\\\nand STS-B (textual similarity, Cer et al. (2017)). The broad coverage makes GLUE benchmark a\\\\nstandard metric to evaluate NLU models such as RoBERTa and DeBERTa. The individual datasets\\\\nare released under different permissive licenses.\\\\nWikiSQL is introduced in Zhong et al. (2017) and contains 56, 355/8, 421 training/validation ex-\\\\namples. The task is to generate SQL queries from natural language questions and table schemata.\\\\nWe encode context as x = {table schema, query} and target as y = {SQL}. The dataset is release\\\\nunder the BSD 3-Clause License.\\\\nSAMSum is introduced in Gliwa et al. (2019) and contains 14, 732/819 training/test examples. It\\\\nconsists of staged chat conversations between two people and corresponding abstractive summaries\\\\nwritten by linguists. We encode context as ”\\\\\\\\n” concatenated utterances followed by a ”\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n”,\\\\nand target as y = {summary}. The dataset is released under the non-commercial licence: Creative\\\\nCommons BY-NC-ND 4.0.\\\\nE2E NLG Challenge was ﬁrst introduced in Novikova et al. (2017) as a dataset for training end-to-\\\\nend, data-driven natural language generation systems and is commonly used for data-to-text evalua-\\\\ntion. The E2E dataset consists of roughly 42, 000 training, 4, 600 validation, and 4, 600 test exam-\\\\nples from the restaurant domain. Each source table used as input can have multiple references. Each\\\\nsample input (x, y) consists of a sequence of slot-value pairs, along with a corresponding natural\\\\nlanguage reference text. The dataset is released under Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0.\\\\nDART is an open-domain data-to-text dataset described in Nan et al. (2020). DART inputs are\\\\nstructured as sequences of ENTITY — RELATION — ENTITY triples. With 82K examples in\\\\ntotal, DART is a signiﬁcantly larger and more complex data-to-text task compared to E2E. The\\\\ndataset is released under the MIT license.\\\\nWebNLG is another commonly used dataset for data-to-text evaluation (Gardent et al., 2017). With\\\\n22K examples in total WebNLG comprises 14 distinct categories, nine of which are seen during\\\\ntraining. Since ﬁve of the 14 total categories are not seen during training, but are represented in\\\\nthe test set, evaluation is typically broken out by “seen” categories (S), “unseen” categories (U)\\\\nand “all” (A). Each input example is represented by a sequence of SUBJECT — PROPERTY —\\\\nOBJECT triples. The dataset is released under Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0.\\\\nD\\\\nHYPERPARAMETERS USED IN EXPERIMENTS\\\\nD.1\\\\nROBERTA\\\\nWe train using AdamW with a linear learning rate decay schedule. The core idea is simple – we cache the kv-cache blocks of processed requests, and reuse these blocks when a new request comes in with the same prefix as previous requests. Since prefix caching is almost a free lunch and won’t change model outputs, it has been widely used by many public endpoints (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) and most open source LLM inference frameworks (e.g., SGLang).\\\\n\\\\nWhile there are many ways to implement prefix caching, vLLM chooses a hash-based approach. Specifically, we hash each kv-cache block by the tokens in the block and the tokens in the prefix before the block:\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\n                    Block 1                  Block 2                  Block 3\\\\n         [A gentle breeze stirred] [the leaves as children] [laughed in the distance]\\\\nBlock 1: |<--- block tokens ---->|\\\\nBlock 2: |<------- prefix ------>| |<--- block tokens --->|\\\\nBlock 3: |<------------------ prefix -------------------->| |<--- block tokens ---->|\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIn the example above, the KV cache in the first block can be uniquely identified with the token “A gentle breeze stirred”. The third block can be uniquely identified with the tokens in the block “laughed in the distance”, along with the prefix tokens “A gentle breeze stirred the leaves as children”. Therefore, we can build the block hash of `hash(tuple[components])`, where components are:\\\\n\\\\n* Parent hash value: The hash value of the parent hash block.\\\\n* Block tokens: A tuple of tokens in this block. The reason to include the exact tokens is to reduce potential hash value collision.\\\\n* Extra hashes: Other values required to make this block unique, such as LoRA IDs, multi-modality input hashes (see the example below), and cache salts to isolate caches in multi-tenant environments.\\\\n\\\\n!!! note \\\\\\\"Note 1\\\\\\\"\\\\n    We only cache full blocks.\\\\n\\\\n!!! note \\\\\\\"Note 2\\\\\\\"\\\\n    In previous versions, the hash key was not guaranteed to be collision-free. As of v0.11, the default hashing algorithm is `sha256`, which addresses collision risks.\\\\n\\\\n    For `vllm serve`, you can control the hashing algorithm via `--prefix-caching-hash-algo`:\\\\n    - `sha256` (default): Uses Python's `pickle` for serialization. Hashes may not be reproducible across different Python or vLLM versions.\\\\n    - `sha256_cbor`: Uses `cbor2` for serialization, providing a reproducible, cross-language compatible hash. This is recommended for deterministic caching across environments.\\\\n    - `xxhash`: `Uses Pickle serialization with xxHash (128-bit) for faster, non-cryptographic hashing. Requires the optional `xxhash` package. IMPORTANT: Use of a hashing algorithm that is not considered cryptographically secure theoretically increases the risk of hash collisions, which can cause undefined behavior or even leak private information in multi-tenant environments. Even if collisions are still very unlikely, it is important to consider your security risk tolerance against the performance benefits before turning this on.\\\\n    - `xxhash_cbor` combines canonical CBOR serialization with xxHash for reproducible hashing. Requires the optional `xxhash` package.    \\\\n\\\\n**A hashing example with multi-modality inputs**  \\\\nIn this example, we illustrate how prefix caching works with multi-modality inputs (e.g., images). Assuming we have a request with the following messages:\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\nmessages = [\\\\n    {\\\\\\\"role\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"user\\\\\\\",\\\\n     \\\\\\\"content\\\\\\\": [\\\\n         {\\\\\\\"type\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"text\\\\\\\",\\\\n          \\\\\\\"text\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"What's in this image?\\\\\\\"\\\\n         },\\\\n         {\\\\\\\"type\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"image_url\\\\\\\",\\\\n          \\\\\\\"image_url\\\\\\\": {\\\\\\\"url\\\\\\\": image_url},\\\\n         },\\\\n    ]},\\\\n]\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIt will become the following prompt:\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\nPrompt:\\\\n    <s>[INST]What's in this image?\\\\\\\\n[IMG][/INST]\\\\n\\\\nTokenized prompt:\\\\n    [1, 3, 7493, 1681, 1294, 1593, 3937, 9551, 10, 4]\\\\n\\\\nPrompt with placeholders (<P>):\\\\n    [1, 3, 7493, 1681, 1294, 1593, 3937, 9551, <P>, <P>, ..., <P>, 4]\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAs we can see, after the tokenization, the `[IMG]` will be replaced by a sequence of placeholder tokens, and these placeholders will be replaced by image embeddings during prefill. The challenge for prefix caching to support this case is we need to differentiate images from the placeholders. To address this problem, we encode the image hash generated by the frontend image processor. For example, the hash of the blocks in the above prompt would be (assuming block size 16, and we have 41 placeholder tokens):\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\nBlock 0\\\\n    Parent hash: None\\\\n    Token IDs: 1, 3, 7493, 1681, 1294, 1593, 3937, 9551, <p>, ..., <p>\\\\n    Extra hash: <image hash>\\\\nBlock 1\\\\n    Parent hash: Block 0 hash\\\\n    Token IDs: <p>, ..., <p>\\\\n    Extra hash: <image hash>\\\\nBlock 2\\\\n    Parent hash: Block 1 hash\\\\n    Token IDs: <p>, ..., <p>\\\\n    Extra hash: <image hash>\\\\nBlock 3\\\\n    Parent hash: Block 2 hash\\\\n    Token IDs: <p>, ..., <p>, 4\\\\n    Extra hash: <image hash>\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIn the rest of this document, we first introduce the data structure used for prefix caching in vLLM v1, followed by the prefix caching workflow of major KV cache operators (e.g., allocate, append, free, eviction). Finally, we use an example to illustrate the end to end prefix caching workflow.\\\\n\\\\n**Cache Isolation for Security**\\\\nTo improve privacy in shared environments, vLLM supports isolating prefix cache reuse through optional per-request salting. By including a `cache_salt` in the request, this value is injected into the hash of the first block, ensuring that only requests with the same salt can reuse cached KV blocks. This prevents timing-based attacks where an adversary could infer cached content by observing latency differences. This offers protection without compromising performance.\\\\n\\\\n```json\\\\n{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"messages\\\\\\\": [\\\\n    {\\\\\\\"role\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"system\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"content\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"You are a helpful assistant.\\\\\\\"},\\\\n    {\\\\\\\"role\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"user\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"content\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Here is a document with details about the world series: ...\\\\\\\"},\\\\n    {\\\\\\\"role\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"user\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"content\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Who won the world series in 2020?\\\\\\\"}\\\\n  ],\\\\n  \\\\\\\"cache_salt\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"your-cache-salt\\\\\\\"\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWith this setup, cache sharing is limited to users or requests that explicitly agree on a common salt, enabling cache reuse within a trust group while isolating others.\\\\n\\\\n## Data Structure\\\\n\\\\nThe prefix caching in vLLM v1 is implemented in the KV cache manager. The basic building block is the “Block” data class (simplified):\\\\n\\\\n```python\\\\nclass KVCacheBlock:\\\\n    # The block ID (immutable)\\\\n    block_id: int\\\\n    # The block hash (will be assigned when the block is full,\\\\n    # and will be reset when the block is evicted).\\\\n    block_hash: BlockHash\\\\n    # The number of requests using this block now.\\\\n    ref_cnt: int\\\\n\\\\n    # The pointers to form a doubly linked list for the free queue.\\\\n    prev_free_block: \\\\\\\"KVCacheBlock | None\\\\\\\" = None\\\\n    next_free_block: \\\\\\\"KVCacheBlock | None\\\\\\\" = None\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThere are two design points to highlight:\\\\n\\\\n1. We allocate all KVCacheBlock when initializing the KV cache manager to be a block pool. This avoids Python object creation overheads and can easily track all blocks all the time.  \\\\n2. We introduce doubly linked list pointers directly in the KVCacheBlock, so that we could construct a free queue directly. This gives us two benefits:  \\\\n    1. We could have O(1) complexity moving elements in the middle to the tail.  \\\\n    2. We could avoid introducing another Python queue (e.g., `deque`) which has a wrapper to the elements.\\\\n\\\\nAs a result, we will have the following components when the KV cache manager is initialized:\\\\n\\\\n![Component Overview](../assets/design/prefix_caching/overview.png)\\\\n\\\\n* Block Pool: A list of KVCacheBlock.  \\\\n* Free Block Queue: Only store the pointers of head and tail blocks for manipulations.  \\\\n* Cache blocks: Mapping from hash key to block IDs.  \\\\n* Request blocks: Mapping from request ID to allocated block IDs.\\\\n\\\\n## Operations\\\\n\\\\n### Block Allocation\\\\n\\\\n**New request:** Workflow for the scheduler to schedule a new request with KV cache block allocation:\\\\n\\\\n1. The scheduler calls `kv_cache_manager.get_computed_blocks()` to get a sequence of blocks that have already been computed. This is done by hashing the prompt tokens in the request and looking up cache blocks.  \\\\n2. The scheduler calls `kv_cache_manager.allocate_slots()`. It does the following steps:  \\\\n    1. Compute the number of new required blocks, and return if there are no sufficient blocks to allocate.  \\\\n    2. “Touch” the computed blocks. It increases the reference count of the computed block by one, and removes the block from the free queue if the block wasn’t used by other requests. This is to avoid these computed blocks being evicted. See the example in the next section for illustration.  \\\\n    3. Allocate new blocks by popping the heads of the free queue. If the head block is a cached block, this also “evicts” the block so that no other requests can reuse it anymore from now on.  \\\\n    4. If an allocated block is already full of tokens, we immediately add it to the cache block, so that the block can be reused by other requests in the same batch.\\\\n\\\\n**Running request:** Workflow for the scheduler to schedule a running request with KV cache block allocation:\\\\n\\\\n1. The scheduler calls `kv_cache_manager.allocate_slots()`. It does the following steps:  \\\\n    1. Compute the number of new required blocks, and return if there are no sufficient blocks to allocate.  \\\\n    2. Allocate new blocks by popping the heads of the free queue. If the head block is a cached block, this also “evicts” the block so that no other requests can reuse it anymore from now on.  \\\\n    3. Append token IDs to the slots in existing blocks as well as the new blocks. If a block is full, we add it to the cache block to cache it.\\\\n\\\\n**Duplicated blocks**  \\\\nAssuming block size is 4 and you send a request (Request 1\\\\\\\\) with prompt ABCDEF and decoding length 3:\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\nPrompt: [A, B, C, D, E, F]\\\\nOutput: [G, H, I]\\\\n\\\\nTime 0:\\\\n  Tokens: [A, B, C, D, E, F, G]\\\\n  Block Table: [0 (ABCD), 1 (EFG)]\\\\n  Cache Blocks: 0\\\\nTime 1:\\\\n  Tokens: [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H]\\\\n  Block Table: [0 (ABCD), 1 (EFGH)]\\\\n  Cache Blocks: 0, 1\\\\nTime 2:\\\\n  Tokens: [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I]\\\\n  Block Table: [0 (ABCD), 1 (EFGH), 2 (I)]\\\\n  Cache Blocks: 0, 1\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nNow block 0 and block 1 are cached, and we send the same request again (Request 2\\\\\\\\) with greedy sampling, so that it will produce exactly the same outputs as the Request 1:\\\\n\\\\n```text\\\\nPrompt: [A, B, C, D, E, F]\\\\nOutput: [G, H, I]\\\\n\\\\nTime 0:\\\\n  Tokens: [A, B, C, D, E, F, G]\\\\n  Block Table: [0 (ABCD), 3 (EFG)]\\\\n  Cache Blocks: 0, 1\\\\nTime 1:\\\\n  Tokens: [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H]\\\\n  Block Table: [0 (ABCD), 3 (EFGH)]\\\\n  Cache Blocks: 0, 1, 3\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAs can be seen, block 3 is a new full block and is cached. However, it is redundant as block 1, meaning that we cached the same block twice. In v0, when detecting block 3 is duplicated, we free block 3 and let Request 2 use block 1 instead, so its block table becomes `[0, 1]` in Time 1. However, the block table in vLLM v1 is append-only, meaning that changing the block table from `[0, 3]` to `[0, 1]` is not allowed. As a result, we will have duplicated blocks for the hash key E-H. This duplication will be eliminated when the request is freed.\\\\n\\\\n### Free\\\\n\\\\nWhen a request is finished, we free all its blocks if no other requests are using them (reference count = 0). In this example, we free request 1 and block 2, 3, 4, 8 associated with it. We can see that the freed blocks are added to the tail of the free queue in the *reverse* order. This is because the last block of a request must hash more tokens and is less likely to be reused by other requests. As a result, it should be evicted first.\\\\n\\\\n![Free queue after a request us freed](../assets/design/prefix_caching/free.png)\\\\n\\\\n### Eviction (LRU)\\\\n\\\\nWhen the head block (least recently used block) of the free queue is cached, we have to evict the block to prevent it from being used by other requests. Specifically, eviction involves the following steps:\\\\n\\\\n1. Pop the block from the head of the free queue. This is the LRU block to be evicted.  \\\\n2. Remove the block ID from the cache block.  \\\\n3. Remove the block hash.\\\\n\\\\n## Example\\\\n\\\\nIn this example, we assume the block size is 4 (each block can cache 4 tokens), and we have 10 blocks in the KV-cache manager in total.\\\\n\\\\n**Time 1: The cache is empty and a new request comes in.** We allocate 4 blocks. 3 of them are already full and cached. The fourth block is partially full with 3 of 4 tokens.\\\\n\\\\n![Example Time 1](../assets/design/prefix_caching/example-time-1.png)\\\\n\\\\n**Time 2: Request 0 makes the block 3 full and asks for a new block to keep decoding.** We cache block 3 and allocate block 4.\\\\n\\\\n![Example Time 2](../assets/design/prefix_caching/example-time-3.png)\\\\n\\\\n**Time 3: Request 1 comes in with the 14 prompt tokens, where the first 10 tokens are the same as request 0.** We can see that only the first 2 blocks (8 tokens) hit the cache, because the 3rd block only matches 2 of 4 tokens.\\\\n\\\\n![Example Time 3](../assets/design/prefix_caching/example-time-4.png)\\\\n\\\\n**Time 4: Request 0 is finished and free.** Blocks 2, 3 and 4 are added to the free queue in the reverse order (but block 2 and 3 are still cached). Block 0 and 1 are not added to the free queue because they are being used by Request 1.\\\\n\\\\n![Example Time 4](../assets/design/prefix_caching/example-time-5.png)\\\\n\\\\n**Time 5: Request 1 is finished and free.**\\\\n\\\\n![Example Time 5](../assets/design/prefix_caching/example-time-6.png)\\\\n\\\\n**Time 6: Request 2 comes in with the 29 prompt tokens, where the first 12 tokens are the same as request 0\\\\\\\\.** Note that even the block order in the free queue was `7 - 8 - 9 - 4 - 3 - 2 - 6 - 5 - 1 - 0`, the cache hit blocks (i.e., 0, 1, 2) are touched and removed from the queue before allocation, so the free queue becomes `7 - 8 - 9 - 4 - 3 - 6 - 5`. As a result, the allocated blocks are 0 (cached), 1 (cached), 2 (cached), 7, 8, 9, 4, 3 (evicted).\\\\n\\\\n![Example Time 6](../assets/design/prefix_caching/example-time-7.png)\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 13926]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 13926, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 13926, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-TORCH-NUMERIC/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"bb6b2d8154a10f8f3b15e5ae4465cbc8d833067046964fc6b4d66dc036131b45\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"\\\\n===== docs/source/notes/numerical_accuracy.rst =====\\\\n.. _numerical_accuracy:\\\\n\\\\nNumerical accuracy\\\\n==================\\\\n\\\\nIn modern computers, floating point numbers are represented using IEEE 754 standard.\\\\nFor more details on floating point arithmetic and IEEE 754 standard, please see\\\\n`Floating point arithmetic <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic>`_\\\\nIn particular, note that floating point provides limited accuracy (about 7 decimal digits\\\\nfor single precision floating point numbers, about 16 decimal digits for double precision\\\\nfloating point numbers) and that floating point addition and multiplication are not\\\\nassociative, so the order of the operations affects the results.\\\\nBecause of this, PyTorch is not guaranteed\\\\nto produce bitwise identical results for floating point computations that are\\\\nmathematically identical. Similarly, bitwise identical results are not guaranteed across\\\\nPyTorch releases, individual commits, or different platforms. In particular, CPU and GPU\\\\nresults can be different even for bitwise-identical inputs and even after controlling for\\\\nthe sources of randomness.\\\\n\\\\nBatched computations or slice computations\\\\n------------------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nMany operations in PyTorch support batched computation, where the same operation is performed\\\\nfor the elements of the batches of inputs. An example of this is :meth:`torch.mm` and\\\\n:meth:`torch.bmm`. It is possible to implement batched computation as a loop over batch elements,\\\\nand apply the necessary math operations to the individual batch elements, for efficiency reasons\\\\nwe are not doing that, and typically perform computation for the whole batch. The mathematical\\\\nlibraries that we are calling, and PyTorch internal implementations of operations can produce\\\\nslightly different results in this case, compared to non-batched computations. In particular,\\\\nlet ``A`` and ``B`` be 3D tensors with the dimensions suitable for batched matrix multiplication.\\\\nThen ``(A@B)[0]`` (the first element of the batched result) is not guaranteed to be bitwise\\\\nidentical to ``A[0]@B[0]`` (the matrix product of the first elements of the input batches)\\\\neven though mathematically it's an identical computation.\\\\n\\\\nSimilarly, an operation applied to a tensor slice is not guaranteed to produce results that are\\\\nidentical to the slice of the result of the same operation applied to the full tensor. E.g. let\\\\n``A`` be a 2-dimensional tensor. ``A.sum(-1)[0]`` is not guaranteed to be bitwise equal to\\\\n``A[:,0].sum()``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nExtremal values\\\\n---------------\\\\n\\\\nWhen inputs contain large values such that intermediate results may overflow the range of the\\\\nused datatype, the end result may overflow too, even though it is representable in the original\\\\ndatatype. E.g.:\\\\n\\\\n.. code:: python\\\\n\\\\n    import torch\\\\n    a=torch.tensor([1e20, 1e20]) # fp32 type by default\\\\n    a.norm() # produces tensor(inf)\\\\n    a.double().norm() # produces tensor(1.4142e+20, dtype=torch.float64), representable in fp32\\\\n\\\\n.. _Linear Algebra Stability:\\\\n\\\\nLinear algebra (``torch.linalg``)\\\\n---------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nNon-finite values\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nThe external libraries (backends) that ``torch.linalg`` uses provide no guarantees on their behaviour\\\\nwhen the inputs have non-finite values like ``inf`` or ``NaN``. As such, neither does PyTorch.\\\\nThe operations may return a tensor with non-finite values, or raise an exception, or even segfault.\\\\n\\\\nConsider using :func:`torch.isfinite` before calling these functions to detect this situation.\\\\n\\\\nExtremal values in linalg\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nFunctions within ``torch.linalg`` have more `Extremal Values`_ than other PyTorch functions.\\\\n\\\\n:ref:`linalg solvers` and :ref:`linalg inverses` assume that the input matrix ``A`` is invertible. If it is close to\\\\nbeing non-invertible (for example, if it has a very small singular value), then these algorithms may silently return\\\\nincorrect results. These matrices are said to be `ill-conditioned <https://nhigham.com/2020/03/19/what-is-a-condition-number/>`_.\\\\nIf provided with ill-conditioned inputs, the result of these functions they may vary when using the same inputs on different\\\\ndevices or when using different backends via the keyword ``driver``.\\\\n\\\\nSpectral operations like ``svd``, ``eig``, and ``eigh`` may also return incorrect results (and their gradients may be infinite)\\\\nwhen their inputs have singular values that are close to each other. This is because the algorithms used to compute these decompositions\\\\nstruggle to converge for these inputs.\\\\n\\\\nRunning the computation in ``float64`` (as NumPy does by default) often helps, but it does not solve these issues in all cases.\\\\nAnalyzing the spectrum of the inputs via :func:`torch.linalg.svdvals` or their condition number via :func:`torch.linalg.cond`\\\\nmay help to detect these issues.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nTensorFloat-32(TF32) on Nvidia Ampere (and later) devices\\\\n---------------------------------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nOn Ampere (and later) Nvidia GPUs, PyTorch can use TensorFloat32 (TF32) to speed up mathematically intensive operations, in particular matrix multiplications and convolutions.\\\\nWhen an operation is performed using TF32 tensor cores, only the first 10 bits of the input mantissa are read.\\\\nThis may reduce accuracy and produce surprising results (e.g., multiplying a matrix by the identity matrix may produce results that are different from the input).\\\\nBy default, TF32 tensor cores are disabled for matrix multiplications and enabled for convolutions, although most neural network workloads have the same convergence behavior when using TF32 as they have with fp32.\\\\nWe recommend enabling TF32 tensor cores for matrix multiplications with ``torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision = \\\\\\\"tf32\\\\\\\"`` (```torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True`` is going to be deprecated) if your network does not need full float32 precision.\\\\nIf your network needs full float32 precision for both matrix multiplications and convolutions, then TF32 tensor cores can also be disabled for convolutions with ``torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision = \\\\\\\"ieee\\\\\\\"`` (``torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False`` is going to be deprecated).\\\\n\\\\nFor more information see :ref:`TensorFloat32<tf32_on_ampere>`.\\\\n\\\\nReduced Precision Reduction for FP16 and BF16 GEMMs\\\\n----------------------------------------------------\\\\nHalf-precision GEMM operations are typically done with intermediate accumulations (reduction) in single-precision for numerical accuracy and improved resilience to overflow. For performance, certain GPU architectures, especially more recent ones, allow a few truncations of the intermediate accumulation results to the reduced precision (e.g., half-precision). This change is often benign from the perspective of model convergence, though it may lead to unexpected results (e.g., ``inf`` values when the final result should be be representable in half-precision).\\\\nIf reduced-precision reductions are problematic, they can be turned off with\\\\n``torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction = False``\\\\n\\\\nA similar flag exists for BF16 GEMM operations and is turned on by default. If BF16\\\\nreduced-precision reductions are problematic, they can be turned off with\\\\n``torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction = False``\\\\n\\\\nFor more information see :ref:`allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction<fp16reducedprecision>` and :ref:`allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction<bf16reducedprecision>`\\\\n\\\\nReduced Precision Reduction for FP16 and BF16 in Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA)\\\\n------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\\\nA naive SDPA math backend, when using FP16/BF16 inputs, can accumulate significant numerical errors due to the usage of low-precision intermediate buffers. To mitigate this issue, the default behavior now involves upcasting FP16/BF16 inputs to FP32. Computations are performed in FP32/TF32, and the final FP32 results are then downcasted back to FP16/BF16. This will improve numerical accuracy of the final output for the math backend with FP16/BF16 inputs, but increases memory usages and may cause the performance regressions in the math backend as computations shift from FP16/BF16 BMM to FP32/TF32 BMM/Matmul.\\\\n\\\\nFor scenarios where reduced-precision reductions are preferred for speed, they can be enabled with the following setting:\\\\n``torch.backends.cuda.allow_fp16_bf16_reduction_math_sdp(True)``\\\\n\\\\n.. _fp16_on_mi200:\\\\n\\\\nReduced Precision FP16 and BF16 GEMMs and Convolutions on AMD Instinct MI200 devices\\\\n------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\\\nOn AMD Instinct MI200 GPUs, the FP16 and BF16 V_DOT2 and MFMA matrix instructions flush input and output denormal values to zero. FP32 and FP64 MFMA matrix instructions do not flush input and output denormal values to zero. The affected instructions are only used by rocBLAS (GEMM) and MIOpen (convolution) kernels; all other PyTorch operations will not encounter this behavior. All other supported AMD GPUs will not encounter this behavior.\\\\n\\\\nrocBLAS and MIOpen provide alternate implementations for affected FP16 operations. Alternate implementations for BF16 operations are not provided; BF16 numbers have a larger dynamic range than FP16 numbers and are less likely to encounter denormal values. For the FP16 alternate implementations, FP16 input values are cast to an intermediate BF16 value and then cast back to FP16 output after the accumulate FP32 operations. In this way, the input and output types are unchanged.\\\\n\\\\nWhen training using FP16 precision, some models may fail to converge with FP16 denorms flushed to zero. Denormal values more frequently occur in the backward pass of training during gradient calculation. PyTorch by default will use the rocBLAS and MIOpen alternate implementations during the backward pass. The default behavior can be overridden using environment variables, ROCBLAS_INTERNAL_FP16_ALT_IMPL and MIOPEN_DEBUG_CONVOLUTION_ATTRIB_FP16_ALT_IMPL. The behavior of these environment variables is as follows:\\\\n\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n|               | forward   | backward  |\\\\n+===============+===========+===========+\\\\n| Env unset     | original  | alternate |\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n| Env set to 1  | alternate | alternate |\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n| Env set to 0  | original  | original  |\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n\\\\nThe following is the list of operations where rocBLAS may be used:\\\\n\\\\n* torch.addbmm\\\\n* torch.addmm\\\\n* torch.baddbmm\\\\n* torch.bmm\\\\n* torch.mm\\\\n* torch.nn.GRUCell\\\\n* torch.nn.LSTMCell\\\\n* torch.nn.Linear\\\\n* torch.sparse.addmm\\\\n* the following torch._C._ConvBackend implementations:\\\\n\\\\n  * slowNd\\\\n  * slowNd_transposed\\\\n  * slowNd_dilated\\\\n  * slowNd_dilated_transposed\\\\n\\\\nThe following is the list of operations where MIOpen may be used:\\\\n\\\\n* torch.nn.Conv[Transpose]Nd\\\\n* the following torch._C._ConvBackend implementations:\\\\n\\\\n  * ConvBackend::Miopen\\\\n  * ConvBackend::MiopenDepthwise\\\\n  * ConvBackend::MiopenTranspose\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 10998]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 10998, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 10998, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-SLORA/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"e06ac1ab6ada0d18e1ed10cda8019138fc8698fbf5bbf138c60257e92f9fcb36\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"=== PDF page 1 ===\\\\nS-LORA: SERVING THOUSANDS OF CONCURRENT LORA ADAPTERS\\\\nYing Sheng * 1 2 Shiyi Cao * 1 Dacheng Li 1 Coleman Hooper 1 Nicholas Lee 1 Shuo Yang 3 Christopher Chou 1\\\\nBanghua Zhu 1 Lianmin Zheng 1 Kurt Keutzer 1 Joseph E. Gonzalez 1 Ion Stoica 1\\\\nABSTRACT\\\\nThe “pretrain-then-finetune” paradigm is commonly adopted in the deployment of large language models. Low-\\\\nRank Adaptation (LoRA), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, is often employed to adapt a base model to a\\\\nmultitude of tasks, resulting in a substantial collection of LoRA adapters derived from one base model. We observe\\\\nthat this paradigm presents significant opportunities for batched inference during serving. To capitalize on these\\\\nopportunities, we present S-LoRA, a system designed for the scalable serving of many LoRA adapters. S-LoRA\\\\nstores all adapters in the main memory and fetches the adapters used by the currently running queries to the\\\\nGPU memory. To efficiently use the GPU memory and reduce fragmentation, S-LoRA proposes Unified Paging.\\\\nUnified Paging uses a unified memory pool to manage dynamic adapter weights with different ranks and KV cache\\\\ntensors with varying sequence lengths. Additionally, S-LoRA employs a novel tensor parallelism strategy and\\\\nhighly optimized custom CUDA kernels for heterogeneous batching of LoRA computation. Collectively, these\\\\nfeatures enable S-LoRA to serve thousands of LoRA adapters on a single GPU or across multiple GPUs with a\\\\nsmall overhead. Compared to state-of-the-art libraries such as HuggingFace PEFT and vLLM (with naive support\\\\nof LoRA serving), S-LoRA can improve the throughput by up to 4 times and increase the number of served\\\\nadapters by several orders of magnitude. As a result, S-LoRA enables scalable serving of many task-specific\\\\nfine-tuned models and offers the potential for large-scale customized fine-tuning services.\\\\n1\\\\nINTRODUCTION\\\\nLarge language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in\\\\nmodern applications, ranging from natural language pro-\\\\ncessing to more general tasks (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron\\\\net al., 2023b; Alayrac et al., 2022). Within these domains,\\\\nLLMs have consistently demonstrated superior performance,\\\\nespecially when fine-tuned for specific tasks (Kenton &\\\\nToutanova, 2019; Houlsby et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2022).\\\\nThis “pretrain-then-finetune” paradigm has led to the pro-\\\\nliferation of numerous fine-tuned variants of a single base\\\\nLLM, each tailored to a specific task or domain.\\\\nWhen scaling the fine-tuning of a base model for numerous\\\\ntasks, such as personalized assistants, the associated train-\\\\ning and serving costs can become substantial. To address\\\\nthis, several parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods have\\\\nbeen developed. A prime exemplar is Low-Rank Adaptation\\\\n(LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021), which enables efficient fine-tuning\\\\nby updating only low-rank additive matrices. These matri-\\\\nces consist of a small number of parameters, referred to as\\\\nadapter weights. LoRA has shown that by fine-tuning just\\\\n*Equal contribution. Part of the work was done when Ying\\\\nwas visiting UC Berkeley.\\\\n1UC Berkeley 2Stanford University\\\\n3Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Correspondence to: Ying Sheng\\\\n<ying1123@stanford.edu>, Shiyi Cao <shicao@berkeley.edu>.\\\\nthese adapter weights, it is possible to achieve performance\\\\non par with full-weight fine-tuning. However, despite con-\\\\nsiderable research into fine-tuning, the question of how to\\\\nserve these fine-tuned variants at scale remains unexplored.\\\\nOne of the key innovations in the LoRA paper was the\\\\nelimination of adapter inference latency by directly merging\\\\nthe adapter with the model parameters. Additionally, to\\\\nsupport multiple models on a single machine, the same\\\\npaper proposes swapping adapters by adding and subtracting\\\\nLoRA weights from the base model. While this approach\\\\nenables low-latency inference for a single adapter and serial\\\\nexecution across adapters, it significantly reduces overall\\\\nserving throughput and increases total latency when serving\\\\nmultiple adapters concurrently. Moreover, the paper does\\\\nnot consider the opportunity to leverage host memory to\\\\nincrease the number of adapters hosted by a single machine.\\\\nIn this paper, we study how to scalably serve thousands\\\\nof LoRA adapters on a single machine. We observe that\\\\nthe shared base model, which underpins numerous LoRA\\\\nadapters, presents a substantial opportunity for batched in-\\\\nference. To achieve high-throughput multi-adapter serving,\\\\nit is advantageous to separate the batchable base model\\\\ncomputation from individual LoRA computations.\\\\nWhile leveraging batching in the base model is straight-\\\\nforward (as all queries share the base model), extending\\\\narXiv:2311.03285v1  [cs.LG]  6 Nov 2023\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 2 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nbatching to the adapters is challenging. First, serving many\\\\nLoRA adapters simultaneously requires efficient memory\\\\nmanagement. Since GPU memory is limited, we must store\\\\nadapter weights outside the GPU and dynamically fetch\\\\nthem when needed. However, dynamically loading and un-\\\\nloading adapters of varying sizes, coupled with the dynamic\\\\nallocation and deallocation of KV cache tensors for requests\\\\nwith different sequence lengths, can lead to significant mem-\\\\nory fragmentation and I/O overhead. Second, apart from\\\\nthe easily batchable base model computation, the separated\\\\ncomputation of many adapters with distinct ranks in non-\\\\ncontiguous memory is challenging to batch and demands the\\\\ndevelopment of new computation kernels. Third, leveraging\\\\nmultiple GPUs on a single machine requires novel paral-\\\\nlelism strategies to accommodate the added LoRA weights\\\\nand computations. It is essential to carefully design this strat-\\\\negy to minimize communication and memory overheads.\\\\nTo this end, we introduce S-LoRA, a scalable LoRA serving\\\\nsystem. S-LoRA exploits batching opportunities, efficiently\\\\nmanages both host and GPU memory, and orchestrates par-\\\\nallelism across multiple GPUs. The primary contributions\\\\nof S-LoRA are summarized as follows:\\\\n• Unified Paging: To reduce memory fragmentation and\\\\nincrease batch size, S-LoRA introduces a unified mem-\\\\nory pool. This pool manages dynamic adapter weights\\\\nand KV cache tensors by a unified paging mechanism.\\\\n• Heterogeneous Batching: To minimize the latency over-\\\\nhead when batching different adapters of varying ranks,\\\\nS-LoRA employs highly optimized custom CUDA ker-\\\\nnels. These kernels operate directly on non-contiguous\\\\nmemory and align with the memory pool design, fa-\\\\ncilitating efficient batched inference for added LoRA\\\\ncomputation.\\\\n• S-LoRA TP: To ensure effective parallelization across\\\\nmultiple GPUs, S-LoRA introduces a novel tensor par-\\\\nallelism strategy. This approach incurs minimal com-\\\\nmunication cost for the added LoRA computation com-\\\\npared to that of the base model. This is realized by\\\\nscheduling communications on small intermediate ten-\\\\nsors and fusing them with the communications of the\\\\nbase model.\\\\nWe evaluate S-LoRA by serving Llama-7B/13B/30B/70B.\\\\nResults show that S-LoRA can serve thousands of LoRA\\\\nadapters on a single GPU or across multiple GPUs with\\\\na small overhead. When compared to the state-of-the-art\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning library, Huggingface PEFT,\\\\nS-LoRA can enhance throughput by up to 30×. In com-\\\\nparison to the high-throughput serving system vLLM using\\\\na naive support of LoRA serving, S-LoRA can improve\\\\nthroughput by up to 4× and increase the number of served\\\\nadapters by several orders of magnitude. The code is avail-\\\\nable at https://github.com/S-LoRA/S-LoRA.\\\\n2\\\\nBACKGROUND\\\\nLow-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) is a\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning method designed to adapt\\\\npre-trained large language models to new tasks. The mo-\\\\ntivation behind LoRA stems from the low intrinsic dimen-\\\\nsionality of model updates during adaptation. In the training\\\\nphase, LoRA freezes the weights of a pre-trained base model\\\\nand adds trainable low-rank matrices to each layer. This\\\\napproach significantly reduces the number of trainable pa-\\\\nrameters and memory consumption. When compared to full\\\\nparameter fine-tuning, LoRA can often reduce the number of\\\\ntrainable parameters by orders of magnitude (e.g., 10000×)\\\\nwhile retaining comparable accuracy. For the inference\\\\nphase, the original paper suggests merging the low-rank\\\\nmatrices with the weights of the base model. As a result,\\\\nthere is no added overhead during inference, setting it apart\\\\nfrom previous adapters like (Houlsby et al., 2019) or prompt\\\\ntuning methods such as (Lester et al., 2021).\\\\nFormally, for a pre-trained weight matrix W ∈Rh×d, LoRA\\\\nintroduces the update as W ′ = W +AB, where A ∈Rh×r,\\\\nB ∈Rr×d, and the rank r ≪min(h, d). If the forward pass\\\\nof a base model is defined by h = xW, then after applying\\\\nLoRA, the forward pass becomes\\\\nh = xW ′ = x(W + AB)\\\\n(1)\\\\n= xW + xAB.\\\\n(2)\\\\nTypically, this adjustment is only applied to the query, key,\\\\nvalue, and output projection matrices in the self-attention\\\\nmodule, excluding the feed-forward module.\\\\nBecause LoRA greatly reduces the training and weight stor-\\\\nage costs, it has been widely adopted by the community,\\\\nand people have created hundreds of thousands of LoRA\\\\nadapters for pre-trained large language models and diffusion\\\\nmodels (Mangrulkar et al., 2022).\\\\n2.1\\\\nServing Large Language Models\\\\nMost large language models (LLMs) are based on the trans-\\\\nformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). The number of\\\\nparameters in an LLM ranges from several billion to several\\\\ntrillion (Brown et al., 2020; Chowdhery et al., 2022; Fedus\\\\net al., 2022), corresponding to disk sizes spanning several gi-\\\\ngabytes to even terabytes. This scale results in LLM serving\\\\nhaving significant computational and memory demands.\\\\nAdditionally, the inference process for LLMs requires iter-\\\\native autoregressive decoding. Initially, the model carries\\\\nout a forward pass to encode the prompt. Following this, it\\\\ndecodes the output one token at a time. The sequential pro-\\\\ncess makes decoding slow. Since each token attends to the\\\\nhidden states of all its preceding tokens, it becomes essential\\\\nto store the hidden states of all previous tokens. This storage\\\\nis referred to as the “KV cache”. Such a mechanism adds to\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 3 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nthe memory overhead and causes the decoding process to\\\\nbe more memory-intensive than computation-intensive.\\\\nThe challenges become even more pronounced in online\\\\nsettings, where requests of varying sequence lengths ar-\\\\nrive dynamically. To accommodate such dynamic incoming\\\\nrequests, Orca (Yu et al., 2022) introduces a method of fine-\\\\ngrained, iteration-level scheduling. Instead of scheduling at\\\\nthe request level, Orca batches at the token level. This ap-\\\\nproach allows for the continuous addition of new requests to\\\\nthe currently running batch, resulting in substantially higher\\\\nthroughput. vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) further optimizes\\\\nOrca’s memory efficiency using PagedAttention. PagedAt-\\\\ntention adopts concepts from virtual memory and paging in\\\\noperating systems and manages the storage and access of\\\\ndynamic KV cache tensors in a paged fashion. This method\\\\nefficiently reduces fragmentation, facilitating larger batch\\\\nsizes and higher throughput.\\\\nWhen serving very large models that exceed the memory\\\\ncapacity of a single GPU, or when there are stringent la-\\\\ntency requirements, it is necessary to parallelize the model\\\\nacross multiple GPUs. Several model parallelism methods\\\\nhave been proposed, such as tensor parallelism (Shoeybi\\\\net al., 2019), sequence parallelism (Korthikanti et al., 2023),\\\\npipeline parallelism (Huang et al., 2019), and their combi-\\\\nnations (Narayanan et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2022).\\\\n3\\\\nOVERVIEW OF S-LORA\\\\nS-LoRA encompasses three principal components of in-\\\\nnovation. In Section 4, we introduce our batching strat-\\\\negy, which decomposes the computation between the base\\\\nmodel and the LoRA adapters. Additionally, we address\\\\nthe challenge of request scheduling, covering aspects like\\\\nadapter clustering and admission control. The ability to\\\\nbatch across concurrent adapters, introduces new challenges\\\\naround memory management. In Section 5, we generalize\\\\nPagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) to Unfied Paging which\\\\nsupport dynamically loading LoRA adapters. This approach\\\\nuses a unified memory pool to store the KV caches and\\\\nadapter weights in a paged fashion, which can reduce frag-\\\\nmentation and balance the dynamic changing size of the\\\\nKV caches and adapter weights. Lastly, in Section 6, we\\\\nintroduce our new tensor parallelism strategy that enables us\\\\nto efficiently decoupled the base model and LoRA adapters.\\\\n4\\\\nBATCHING AND SCHEDULING\\\\n4.1\\\\nBatching\\\\nOur batching strategy aims to support online and high-\\\\nthroughput serving of many LoRA adapters simultaneously.\\\\nFor a single adapter, the method recommended by (Hu et al.,\\\\n2021) is to merge the adapter weights into the base model\\\\nW\\\\nx1\\\\nx2\\\\nx3\\\\nx\\\\nA\\\\n1\\\\nB1\\\\nx1\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx2\\\\nA\\\\n2\\\\nB2\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx3\\\\nA\\\\n3\\\\nB3\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nBatched base computation\\\\nBatched LoRA computation\\\\nadd\\\\nFigure 1. This has the\\\\nadvantage that there is no additional adapter overhead during\\\\ninference, since the new model has the same number of\\\\nparameters as the base model. In fact, this was a prominent\\\\nfeature of the original LoRA work.\\\\nHowever, when there are multiple adapters, merging the\\\\nweights into the base model leads to multiple weight copies\\\\nand missed batching opportunities. Directly merging the\\\\nmodels requires maintaining many copies of the full lan-\\\\nguage model. In the original LoRA paper, the authors pro-\\\\nposed adding and subtracting LoRA weights on the fly to\\\\nenable serving multiple models without increasing the mem-\\\\nory overhead. However, this approach doesn’t support con-\\\\ncurrent inference on separate LoRA adapters and therefore\\\\nlimits batching opportunities.\\\\nIn this paper, we show that merging LoRA adapters into\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 4 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nthe base model is inefficient for the multi-LoRA high-\\\\nthroughput serving setting. Instead, we propose computing\\\\nthe LoRA computation xAB on-the-fly as shown in Eq. 2.\\\\nThis avoids weight duplication and enables batching of the\\\\nmore costly xW operation. But this approach also increases\\\\nthe computation overhead. However, because the cost of\\\\nxAB is substantially lower than xW and there is a consid-\\\\nerable savings from batching xW across different adapters,\\\\nwe show that the savings far exceed the additional overhead.\\\\nUnfortunately, directly implementing the factored computa-\\\\ntion of the base model and individual LoRA adapters using\\\\nthe batch GEMM kernel from the existing BLAS libraries\\\\nwould require significant padding and result in poor hard-\\\\nware utilization. This is because of the heterogeneity of\\\\nsequence lengths and adapter ranks.\\\\nIn S-LoRA, we batch the computation of the base model and\\\\nthen employ custom CUDA kernels to execute the additional\\\\nxAB for all adapters separately. This process is illustrated\\\\nby Figure 1. Instead of naively using padding and using the\\\\nbatch GEMM kernel from the BLAS library for the LoRA\\\\ncomputation, we implement custom CUDA kernels for more\\\\nefficient computation without padding. In Subsection 5.3,\\\\nwe discuss the implementation details.\\\\nWhile the number of LoRA adapters can be large if we\\\\nstore them in main memory, the number of LoRA adapters\\\\nneeded for the currently running batch is manageable, be-\\\\ncause the batch size is bounded by the GPU memory. To\\\\ntake advantage of this, we store all LoRA adapters in the\\\\nmain memory and fetch only the LoRA adapters needed\\\\nfor the currently running batch to the GPU RAM when\\\\nrunning the inference for that batch. In this case, the max-\\\\nimum number of adapters that can be served is bounded\\\\nby the main memory size. This process is illustrated by\\\\nFigure 2. To achieve high-throughput serving, we adopt the\\\\niteration-level scheduling batching strategy from Orca (Yu\\\\net al., 2022). In this approach, requests are scheduled at the\\\\ntoken level. We immediately incorporate a new request into\\\\nthe running batch if space is available. The request will exit\\\\nthe batch once it reaches the maximum number of gener-\\\\nated tokens or fulfills other stopping criteria. This process\\\\nreduces GPU memory usage but introduces new memory\\\\nmanagement challenges. In Section 5, we will discuss our\\\\ntechniques to manage memory efficiently.\\\\n4.2\\\\nAdapter Clustering\\\\nTo enhance batching efficiency, one potential strategy is\\\\nreducing the number of active adapters in a running batch.\\\\nBy using fewer adapters, there is an opportunity to allocate\\\\nmore memory to the KV cache, which in turn can facili-\\\\ntate larger batch sizes. Given the common memory capaci-\\\\nties of GPUs, they are often underutilized while decoding.\\\\nConsequently, increasing the batch size can lead to higher\\\\nthroughput. A direct approach to reducing the number of\\\\nadapters in a running batch is to prioritize batching requests\\\\nthat use the same adapter, a strategy we term “adapter clus-\\\\ntering”. However, adapter clustering comes with its own set\\\\nof trade-offs. For example, it can hurt the average latency\\\\nor fairness among adapters. We provide an ablation study in\\\\nAppendix A to illustrate how throughput and latency change\\\\naccording to the cluster size.\\\\n4.3\\\\nAdmission Control\\\\nIn S-LoRA, we also applied an admission control strategy\\\\nto sustain good attainment when the traffic is higher than the\\\\nserving system capacity. A serving system is typically char-\\\\nacterized by a service level objective (SLO) which specifies\\\\nthe desired latency of processing requests. If the serving\\\\nsystem has fixed capacity, it must implement an admission\\\\ncontrol mechanism, that drops a request, if the system can-\\\\nnot meet its SLO. Otherwise, if no request is dropped, and\\\\nthe number of incoming requests is larger than the system\\\\ncapacity for long enough, the serving system is bound to\\\\nviolate the SLO. We implemented an abort strategy to mimic\\\\nadmission control in S-LoRA, called early abort strategy.\\\\nIntuitively, we estimate the set of latest requests that we\\\\ncan serve in SLO, and then serve them in the order of ar-\\\\nrival time. More implementation details and mathematical\\\\njustifications are deferred to Appendix B.\\\\n5\\\\nMEMORY MANAGEMENT\\\\nCompared to serving a single base model, serving multiple\\\\nLoRA adapters simultaneously presents new memory man-\\\\nagement challenges. To support many adapters, S-LoRA\\\\nstores them in the main memory and dynamically loads the\\\\nadapter weights needed for the currently running batch into\\\\nGPU RAM. During this process, there are two noticeable\\\\nchallenges. The first is memory fragmentation, resulting\\\\nfrom the dynamic loading and offloading adapter weights of\\\\nvarious sizes. The second is the latency overhead introduced\\\\nby adapter loading and offloading. To tackle these chal-\\\\nlenges efficiently, we propose Unfied Paging and overlap\\\\nthe I/O with computation by prefetching adapter weights.\\\\n5.1\\\\nUnified Paging\\\\nUnderstanding the nature of adapter weights is essential for\\\\noptimizing memory usage. Our primary observation is that\\\\nthese dynamic adapter weights are analogous to dynamic\\\\nKV caches in several ways:\\\\n• Variable sizes and operations: Just as the size of\\\\nKV cache size fluctuates with the sequence length, the\\\\nranks of the active adapters can also depend on the\\\\nchoice of adapter associated with each request. KV\\\\ncaches are allocated when requests arrive and deal-\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 5 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nKV caches\\\\nAdapter weights\\\\nEmpty\\\\nH\\\\nFigure 3. Unified memory pool. We use a unified memory pool to\\\\nstore both KV caches and adapter weights in a non-contiguous way\\\\nto reduce memory fragmentation. The page size is H elements.\\\\nlocated once the requests are completed. Similarly,\\\\nadapter weights are loaded and cleared with each re-\\\\nquest. If not managed properly, this variability can\\\\nresult in fragmentation.\\\\n• Dimensionality: A KV cache tensor for a request in\\\\na layer has a shape of (S, H), where S denotes the se-\\\\nquence length and H represents the hidden dimension.\\\\nMeanwhile, the shape of a LoRA weight is (R, H),\\\\nwith R standing for the rank and H the hidden dimen-\\\\nsion. Both share a dimension size of H that can be\\\\nleveraged to reduce fragmentation.\\\\nMotivated by these parallels, we extend the idea of Page-\\\\ndAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) to Unified Paging which\\\\nmanages adapter weights in addition to the KV cache. Uni-\\\\nfied Paging uses a unified memory pool to jointly manage\\\\nboth KV cache and adapter weights. To implement this, we\\\\nfirst allocate a large buffer statically for the memory pool.\\\\nThis buffer uses all available space except for the space oc-\\\\ncupied by the base model weights and temporary activation\\\\ntensors. Both KV caches and adapter weights are stored in\\\\nthis memory pool in a paged manner, with each page corre-\\\\nsponding to a vector of H. Thus, a KV cache tensor with a\\\\nsequence length of S uses up S pages, while a LoRA weight\\\\ntensor of rank R takes up R pages. Figure 3 illustrates the\\\\nlayout of our memory pool, where KV caches and adapter\\\\nweights are stored interleaved and non-contiguously. This\\\\napproach significantly reduces fragmentation, ensuring that\\\\nadapters weights of various ranks can coexist with dynamic\\\\nKV caches in a structured and systematic manner.\\\\n5.2\\\\nPrefetching and Overlapping\\\\nAlthough the unified memory pool mitigates fragmentation,\\\\nthe I/O overhead from loading and offloading remains a\\\\nconcern—especially when dealing with numerous or large\\\\nadapters. The latency introduced by waiting to load these\\\\nadapters can compromise the efficiency of the system.\\\\nTo proactively address this issue, we introduce a dynamic\\\\nprediction mechanism. While running the current decoding\\\\nbatch, we predict the adapters required for the next batch\\\\nbased on the current waiting queue. This prediction allows\\\\nus to prefetch and store them in available memory. Such a\\\\nforward-looking strategy keeps most of the adapters needed\\\\nfor the next batch already in place before running it, which\\\\nreduces I/O time for adapter swapping.\\\\n5.3\\\\nCustom Kernels for heterogeneous LoRA batching\\\\non Non-Contiguous Memory\\\\nDue to the design of the unified memory pool, the adapter\\\\nweights are stored in non-contiguous memory. To run com-\\\\nputations efficiently under this design, we implement cus-\\\\ntom CUDA kernels that support batching LoRA compu-\\\\ntations with varying ranks and sequence lengths in a non-\\\\ncontiguous memory layout. In the prefill stage, the kernel\\\\nhandles a sequence of tokens and gathers adapter weights\\\\nwith different ranks from the memory pool. We call this\\\\nkernel Multi-size Batched Gather Matrix-Matrix Multipli-\\\\ncation (MBGMM). It is implemented in Triton (Tillet et al.,\\\\n2019) with tiling. In the decode stage, the kernel handles\\\\na single token and gathers adapter weights with different\\\\nranks from the memory pool. We call this kernel Multi-size\\\\nBatched Gather Matrix-Vector Multiplication (MBGMV).\\\\nIt is modified from Punica (Chen, 2023) to support multiple\\\\nranks in a batch and more fine-grained memory gathering.\\\\n6\\\\nTENSOR PARALLELISM\\\\nWe design novel tensor parallelism strategies for batched\\\\nLoRA inference to support multi-GPU inference of large\\\\ntransformer models.\\\\nTensor parallelism is the most\\\\nwidely used parallelism method because its single-program\\\\nmultiple-data pattern simplifies its implementation and inte-\\\\ngration with existing systems. Tensor parallelism can reduce\\\\nthe per-GPU memory usage and latency when serving large\\\\nmodels. In our setting, the additional LoRA adapters intro-\\\\nduce new weight matrices and matrix multiplications, which\\\\ncalls for new partition strategies for these added items.\\\\n6.1\\\\nPartition Strategy\\\\nSince the base model uses the Megatron-LM tensor paral-\\\\nlelism strategy (Shoeybi et al., 2019), our approach aims\\\\nto align the partition strategies of inputs and outputs of the\\\\nadded LoRA computation with those of the base model.\\\\nIn this way, we can minimize the communication costs\\\\nby avoiding unnecessary communications and fusing some\\\\ncommunications.\\\\nWe use the feed-forward module (2-layer MLP) to illus-\\\\ntrate our partition strategy. SLO attainment is defined as the percentage\\\\nof requests that return the first token in 6 seconds. Addi-\\\\ntionally, we introduce a new metric termed user satisfaction\\\\n(see Appendix B), which offers a more fine-grained analysis\\\\nof the first token latency. Intuitively, a shorter first token\\\\nlatency gives a higher satisfaction. The satisfaction becomes\\\\n0 if the first token latency exceeds the SLO.\\\\n7.2\\\\nEnd-to-End Results on Synthetic Workloads\\\\nWorkload trace. We generate synthetic workload traces\\\\nusing the Gamma process. Given n adapters, the requests for\\\\nadapter i are modeled using a Gamma arrival process with\\\\na mean rate of λi and a coefficient of variance (CV) of cv.\\\\nThe mean rate, λi, adheres to a power-law distribution with\\\\nan exponent α. The total request rate for all adapters is R\\\\nrequests per second. For the n adapters, we set their ranks\\\\nbased on the list provided in Table 1 with a round-robin\\\\nmethod. Our tests cover various combinations of n, α, R,\\\\nand cv. For every request, the input and output lengths are\\\\nsampled from uniform distributions U[Il, Iu] and U[Ol, Ou]\\\\nrespectively. The default duration of a trace is 5 minutes. To\\\\nconduct comprehensive experiments, we first pick a set of\\\\ndefault parameters for generating workloads, as shown in\\\\nTable 2. When the number of adapters increases,\\\\nthe throughput of S-LoRA initially experiences a slight de-\\\\ncline due to the overhead introduced by LoRA. We construct real-world serving\\\\ntraces by downsampling from the traces of LMSYS Chatbot\\\\nArena (Zheng et al., 2023b;a), a website that serves multiple\\\\nLLMs. The raw log from Arena does not concern LoRA\\\\nadapters; it focuses on different base models. This means the strong performance S-LoRA holds\\\\nfor real world workloads.\\\\n7.4\\\\nMulti-GPU Tensor Parallelism\\\\nWe test the scalability of our tensor parallelism strategy by\\\\nrunning 1) Llama-30B on two A100 (40GB) and four A100\\\\n(40GB) GPUs with 10 to 100 adapters; and 2) Llama-70B\\\\non two A100 (80GB) and four A100 (80GB) GPUs with 10\\\\nadapters. We then report the serving throughputs.\\\\nAs depicted in Figure 8, the disparity between S-LoRA\\\\nwith and without LoRA communication is small. This sug-\\\\ngests that the added LoRA communication in our strategy\\\\nhas a very small overhead. The figure further reveals that\\\\nthe communication overhead due to LoRA is less than the\\\\ncomputational overhead it introduces. Furthermore, when\\\\ntransitioning from 2 GPUs to 4 GPUs, the serving through-\\\\nput increases by more than 2 times. This significant increase\\\\ncan be attributed to the fact that the system is predominantly\\\\nmemory-bound in this context. Adding more GPUs alle-\\\\nviates memory constraints, leading to superlinear scaling.\\\\nIn conclusion, the results verify both the minimal overhead\\\\nand the scalability of our tensor parallelism strategy.\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n2xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n2xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\n0\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\nThroughput (req/s)\\\\nS-LoRA\\\\nS-LoRA (w/o LoRA communication)\\\\nS-LoRA (base only)\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n2xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=100\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n4xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=100\\\\n0\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\nLlama-70B\\\\n2xA100(80GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\nLlama-70B\\\\n4xA100(80GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.5\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.5\\\\n2.0\\\\n2.5\\\\n3.0\\\\n3.5\\\\nFigure 8. Throughput with tensor parallelism.\\\\n7.5\\\\nAblation Study\\\\nMerging adapter weights versus computing on-the-fly.\\\\nWhile S-LoRA does not merge adapter weights and com-\\\\nputes LoRA matrices on-the-fly each time, we compare it\\\\nwith an alternative design that merges an adapter with the\\\\nbase model, denoted as x(W + AB), as proposed in the\\\\nLoRA paper. This approach involves: 1) Updating the base\\\\nmodel with the current adapter weights before each new\\\\nbatch; and 2) Switching to a new adapter if there are too\\\\nmany waiting requests.2 This method is efficient for a small\\\\nnumber of adapters due to the reduced LoRA computation\\\\noverhead.\\\\nResults in Figure 9 demonstrate that with just one adapter,\\\\nthe merging approach outperforms the on-the-fly computa-\\\\ntion owing to a one-time merging cost. However, its per-\\\\nformance declines with more than 2 adapters, primarily\\\\nbecause of the time-consuming switch between adapters.\\\\nSuch switching results in periods of GPU under-utilization.\\\\nFurthermore, a smaller value of α causes requests to be\\\\ndistributed unevenly across adapters, which in turn reduces\\\\nbatch sizes and overall performance.\\\\nEarly abort strategy experiments.\\\\nWe compared S-\\\\nLoRA’s early abort strategy to First Come First Serve\\\\n(FCFS) and Last Come First Serve (LCFS) for optimiz-\\\\ning user satisfaction and SLO attainment. As shown in\\\\nFigure 10, S-LoRA-Abort outperforms both, especially as\\\\ncv scales. FCFS is least effective, often processing requests\\\\nthat have already missed the SLO. LCFS, similar to a greedy\\\\nalgorithm that only prioritizes the newest requests, works\\\\nwell for small cv, but its performance drops with larger\\\\n2This is different from PEFT. For example, it has continuous\\\\nbatching and PagedAttention, which are not enabled in PEFT.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 10 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\nnumber of adapters\\\\n1.1\\\\n1.2\\\\n1.3\\\\n1.4\\\\n1.5\\\\n1.6\\\\n1.7\\\\n1.8\\\\nthroughput (req/s)\\\\nS-LoRA-merge alpha=0.1\\\\nS-LoRA alpha=0.1\\\\nS-LoRA-merge alpha=1\\\\nS-LoRA alpha=1\\\\nFigure 9. S-LoRA-Abort excels as it avoids prioritizing only the\\\\nnewest requests, as detailed in Appendix B.\\\\n8\\\\nRELATED WORK\\\\nOptimize LLM serving with system techniques. The sig-\\\\nnificance of the transformer architecture has led to the devel-\\\\nopment of many specialized serving systems for it. These\\\\nsystems use advanced batching mechanisms (Fang et al.,\\\\n2021; Yu et al., 2022), memory optimizations (Sheng et al.,\\\\n2023; Kwon et al., 2023), GPU kernel optimizations (Wang\\\\net al., 2021; Aminabadi et al., 2022; NVIDIA, 2023; Dao,\\\\n2023), model parallelism (Pope et al., 2022; Aminabadi\\\\net al., 2022), parameter sharing (Zhou et al., 2022), and\\\\nspeculative execution (Stern et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2023)\\\\nfor efficient serving. Among them, PetS (Zhou et al., 2022)\\\\nis most relevant to ours. However, PetS only considers\\\\nthe serving for small encoder-only BERT models. It does\\\\nnot consider generative inference, a very large number of\\\\nadapters or large models go beyond a single GPU, so it does\\\\nnot address the problems in our settings.\\\\nIn a concurrent work (Chen et al., 2023), the concept of\\\\ndecomposed computation for the base model and adapters\\\\nwas explored. Our CUDA kernels were developed based\\\\non the implementation presented in a prior blog post of this\\\\nstudy, with additional support for batching different ranks\\\\nand non-contiguous memory. Moreover, our novel memory\\\\nmanagement and tensor parallelism techniques have not\\\\nbeen covered in any previous work.\\\\nOptimize LLM serving with algorithm techniques. In\\\\naddition to system-level improvements, inference efficiency\\\\ncan be enhanced using algorithm techniques like quanti-\\\\nzation (Yao et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2022; Frantar\\\\net al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023), sparsifi-\\\\ncation (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023; Zhang et al., 2023b) and\\\\nmodel architecture improvements (Shazeer, 2019). These\\\\napproaches can reduce memory consumption and accelerate\\\\nthe computation, with a minor compromise in model quality.\\\\nThey are complementary to the techniques in this paper.\\\\nParameter-efficient fine-tuning. Recent work has devel-\\\\noped methods for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large\\\\npre-trained language models. These methods show fine-\\\\ntuning is possible with only a small fraction of tuned param-\\\\neters. The state-of-the-art methods include LoRA (Hu et al.,\\\\n2021), Prefix-tuning (Li & Liang, 2021), P-Tuning (Liu\\\\net al., 2021), Prompt tuning (Liu et al., 2023; Lester et al.,\\\\n2021), AdaLoRA (Zhang et al., 2022), and (IA)3 (Liu et al.,\\\\n2022). While our paper focuses on LoRA due to its wide\\\\nadoption, most techniques can be easily applied to other\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning methods as well.\\\\nGeneral purpose model serving systems. Over the years,\\\\nthe domain of general model serving has seen significant\\\\nadvancements, Notable systems from earlier research in-\\\\nclude Clipper (Crankshaw et al., 2017), TensorFlow Serv-\\\\ning (Olston et al., 2017), Nexus (Shen et al., 2019), Infer-\\\\nLine (Crankshaw et al., 2020), and Clockwork (Gujarati\\\\net al., 2020). These systems delve into topics such as batch-\\\\ning, caching, and model placement, catering to both individ-\\\\nual and multiple model deployments. In more recent devel-\\\\nopments, DVABatch (Cui et al., 2022), REEF (Han et al.,\\\\n2022), Shepherd (Zhang et al., 2023a) and AlpaServe (Li\\\\net al., 2023) have explored the ideas of multi-entry multi-\\\\nexit batching, preemption, and statistical multiplexing with\\\\nmodel parallelism. Although these systems have made sig-\\\\nnificant contributions, they overlook the auto-regressive\\\\ncharacteristics and parameter-efficient adapters in LLM serv-\\\\ning, leading to potential optimization gaps.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 11 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\n9\\\\nCONCLUSION\\\\nWe present S-LoRA, a system capable of serving thou-\\\\nsands of LoRA adapters from a single machine with much\\\\nhigher throughput compared to existing systems. S-LoRA\\\\nis made possible by our innovative design of the unified\\\\nmemory pool, tensor parallelism strategy, adapter batch-\\\\ning, and CUDA kernels. S-LoRA enables large-scale, cus-\\\\ntomized fine-tuning services essential for deploying models\\\\ntailored to diverse requirements. Future extensions of S-\\\\nLoRA will encompass support for additional adapter meth-\\\\nods, enhanced fused kernels, and the use of multiple CUDA\\\\nstreams to parallelize base model and LoRA computations.\\\\n10\\\\nACKNOWLEDGMENT\\\\nThis research was supported by gifts from Anyscale, As-\\\\ntronomer, Google, IBM, Intel, Lacework, Microsoft, Mo-\\\\nhamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Sam-\\\\nsung SDS, Uber, and VMware. Here for LoRA\\\\nserving, we assume a soft threshold characterized by the\\\\nuser’s reward function. For illustration purposes, let the\\\\narrival time of the requests be integers, and assume that\\\\nwe process one query in each time period of length 1. Let\\\\nQ = {q1, q2, · · · qn} be the request queue in the ascending\\\\norder of the arrival time, and l be the desired number of\\\\nserved requests. We quantify the user’s satisfaction with a\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 16 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nreward function r : R+ 7→[0, 1] that maps the first token\\\\nlatency of a request to a scalar in between [0, 1], where 0\\\\nrepresents the user losing patience and giving up the query,\\\\nand 1 represents the user is completely satisfied with the\\\\nlatency. Let ti be the latency of serving the request qi in the\\\\nqueue Q. Then we aim to solve the following constrained\\\\noptimization:\\\\nmax\\\\nn\\\\nX\\\\ni=1\\\\nr(ti)\\\\n(3)\\\\ns.t. 1(r(ti) > 0) = l.\\\\nWe show that when the derivative of reward is non-\\\\nincreasing, the optimal solution to the above constrained\\\\noptimization problem is to serve the most recent l elements\\\\nqn−l+1, qn−l+2, · · · , qn in order.\\\\nTheorem B.1. Assume that r′(t) ≤0 for any t ∈R+. The\\\\noptimal solution to Equation (3) is to serve the most recent\\\\nl elements qn−l+1, qn−l+2, · · · , qn in order.\\\\nThe proof is deferred to Appendix B.1. In practice, for a\\\\ngiven request queue, we can estimate the largest possible\\\\nnumber of requests to be served in SLO as l. Then we\\\\ntake the most recent l elements for serving. Such an l can\\\\nbe approximated by simulating a First-Come-First-Serve\\\\n(FCFS) strategy, which is optimized to serve requests as\\\\nmany as possible.\\\\nIn S-LoRA, the scenario is more complicated because of the\\\\nheterogeneity and unpredictability of the sequence length.\\\\nAs an approximation, we implement a heuristic as follows.\\\\nThe high-level scheduling is that we will fetch a minibatch\\\\nof new requests to be added into the running batch every\\\\nseveral decode step. From the history, we use the moving\\\\naverage to estimate a current request rate R1 measured in\\\\nhow many requests will be added to the waiting queue per\\\\nperiod of fetching new requests. We also use the moving\\\\naverage to estimate the number of new requests R2 that can\\\\nbe added to the running batch for a period. Let rti be the\\\\ncoming time of request ri, ct be the current time, tlmax be\\\\nthe maximum allowed first token latency to meet the SLO\\\\nand lprefill be the maximum prefill latency for a minibatch\\\\nin history. Each time we generate the new minibatch, we\\\\nwill first abort the requests R = {rk | ct −rtk + lprefill >\\\\ntlmax}. Requests in R are highly likely to miss the SLO\\\\neven if they get scheduled immediately due to the high\\\\nprefill latency. Then if R1 > R2, which means the system\\\\nis temporarily overloaded, we will fetch the newest requests\\\\ninto the minibatch. If R1 ≤R2, the waiting queue will be\\\\nshortened if the trend continues. In this case, we will choose\\\\nfrom the earliest.\\\\nB.1\\\\nProof of Theorem B.1\\\\nWe first prove that for any admission control strategy that\\\\nserves l elements, one can always find another admission\\\\ncontrol strategy that serves the most recent l elements with\\\\na larger cumulative reward.\\\\nAssume that we serve l elements qs1, qs2, · · · , qsl in the l\\\\ntimesteps. Now at the time of serving qs1, we\\\\nserve qk rather than qs1, and keep the rest of the choices in\\\\nother time steps same. In this case, the number of served\\\\nqueries remains the same. On the other hand, we know that\\\\nthe latency satisfies ts1 > tk since the k-th element is more\\\\nrecent.
